title: Myths About Learning Languages
description: A podcast about language myths, a conversation between two learners, an interview with a linguist and a talk about effective study habits.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Podcast: Three big myths
parts.intro: You will hear the host of a podcast about language learning.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Word by Word. Today I want to look at some popular beliefs about learning languages, and ask whether they're actually true.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Myth number one: children learn languages faster than adults. It's a very common belief, and there's some truth in it. Young children often develop a more natural accent. But in the classroom, adults and teenagers usually make faster progress at the start, because they can use logic and already know how learning works.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Myth number two: you have to live in the country to become fluent. Living abroad certainly helps, but it isn't magic. I've met people who spent ten years in another country and still spoke only a little, because they lived in a community where they never needed the local language.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Myth number three is my favourite: some people just don't have a talent for languages. I hear this all the time, and I think it's mostly an excuse. Success depends far more on how regularly you practise than on any special gift.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Of course, talent plays a small part. Some people notice sounds more easily than others. But motivation and habit matter much more, and unlike talent, you can improve both of them.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: After the break, I'll be talking to two listeners who learned a new language as adults, so stay with us.

parts.title: Part 2 · Two learners compare experiences
parts.intro: You will hear two friends, Nam and Sarah, talking about their language studies.

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: Nam, how's your German coming along? Last time we spoke, you were thinking about giving up.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Well, I nearly did. I'd been using an app for six months, and I felt that I was learning lots of words but still couldn't have a conversation.

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: That's exactly what happened to me with Spanish. I could name every fruit in the shop, but when the shopkeeper asked me a question, I froze.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: So what changed things for you?

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: I found a tutor online, a young woman in Madrid. We talk for half an hour twice a week, and at first I made so many mistakes that I was embarrassed. But she kept saying that mistakes are how you learn, and eventually I stopped worrying.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I think the fear of mistakes is my biggest problem. At school, a wrong answer meant a bad mark, so I still feel nervous.

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: Try to think of it differently. A child who says something wrong gets a smile, not a red pen. Speaking badly is simply the way to start speaking well.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: You're right. Perhaps I'll book a tutor, too. Could you send me her details?

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: Of course. She's very patient. And she also helped me to set realistic goals, like ordering a meal or describing my weekend, instead of aiming to be perfect.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That sounds much more manageable. Thanks, Sarah. I feel more motivated already.

parts.title: Part 3 · Interview with a linguist
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Hoa, interviewing a linguist, Professor Mark Hill.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: Professor Hill, many people believe that learning a second language confuses children. Is there any truth in that?

script.speaker: Mark
script.text: Very little, I'm happy to say. Children who grow up with two languages may mix them up for a short time, and may start speaking slightly later. But within a few years they usually catch up, and research suggests they actually have some advantages, such as switching attention between tasks.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: Is it possible to become completely fluent as an adult?

script.speaker: Mark
script.text: It depends what you mean by fluent. If you mean sounding exactly like a native speaker, that's rare, and probably unnecessary. If you mean communicating confidently and being respected, then definitely. Many adult learners reach that level, especially if they find opportunities to speak.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: What about the idea that translation is a useful way to learn?

script.speaker: Mark
script.text: Here, I'd be more cautious. Translating every word in your head slows you down, and languages don't match one to one. A word in English may need three different words in Vietnamese, depending on the context. It's better to learn phrases in situations rather than isolated vocabulary lists.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: Can watching films in the language help?

script.speaker: Mark
script.text: Yes, but not passively. If you only read the subtitles in your own language, you aren't learning much. I'd suggest using subtitles in the language you are studying, and pausing to repeat sentences aloud.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: So what is the single most useful habit?

script.speaker: Mark
script.text: Without question, regular contact. Twenty minutes every day is worth more than a three-hour session on Sunday. The brain consolidates language while we sleep, so a little and often really does work best.

parts.title: Part 4 · Talk: Making a study plan
parts.intro: You will hear a language teacher, Mr Minh, talking to new students at a language school.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Welcome to the course, everyone. I'd like to begin by saying something that may sound strange from a teacher: no course can teach you a language on its own. What I can do is give you tools, and the real learning happens in your own time.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: So let me suggest a simple plan. First, decide on a regular time. Many students say they will study when they have time, but of course, they never have time. If you decide that every morning at seven you'll do fifteen minutes, it becomes automatic, like brushing your teeth.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Second, mix different skills. Listen to a podcast on the bus, read a short article at lunchtime, and write three sentences in a diary before bed. Variety keeps you interested, and each skill supports the others.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Third, speak from the beginning. I know some of you will feel shy, but you will notice your confidence growing faster than you expect. Our school runs a conversation club on Thursday evenings, and I strongly recommend it.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Fourth, be patient. There will be days when you feel that you are making no progress. This is called a plateau, and almost every learner experiences it. It often comes just before a sudden jump forward, so don't give up.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Finally, keep a record of your achievements. At the end of each month, write down what you can now do that you couldn't do before. It's surprisingly motivating.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Now, please take the sheet on your desk and write down your study time. We'll share our plans in groups of three.

questions.text: According to the host, what is true about young children?
options: They always learn faster than adults in class.
They never make mistakes when they speak.
They often develop a more natural accent.
questions.explanation: Young children often develop a more natural accent, but adults often progress faster in class.

evidence.quote: Young children often develop a more natural accent

questions.text: Why do adults and teenagers often progress faster at first?
options: They have better teachers and smaller classes.
They can use logic and already know how to learn.
They have more free time to practise every day.
questions.explanation: The host says they can use logic and already know how learning works.

evidence.quote: they can use logic and already know how learning works

questions.text: Why did some people not learn the language after ten years abroad?
options: They disliked the culture and never made friends.
They never needed the language in their community.
They studied a different language from the local one.
questions.explanation: They lived in a community where they never needed the local language.

evidence.quote: they never needed the local language

questions.text: What does the host think about the idea of "no talent for languages"?
options: It is a scientific fact.
It is completely true.
It is mostly an excuse.
questions.explanation: She calls it mostly an excuse; regular practice matters more.

evidence.quote: I think it's mostly an excuse

questions.text: What is the main idea of this part?
options: Adults cannot learn languages as well as children
Common beliefs about languages are exaggerated
Everyone should live abroad for at least ten years
questions.explanation: The host examines three popular beliefs and shows they are only partly true.

questions.text: What problem did Nam have with his app?
options: It was too difficult for him to use every day
He could not afford to renew it after six months
He learned words but could not speak to people
questions.explanation: He felt he learned many words but could not have a conversation.

questions.text: What happened to Sarah in the Spanish shop?
options: She argued with the shopkeeper about the price
She bought the wrong fruit and felt embarrassed
She froze when the shopkeeper spoke to her
questions.explanation: She knew every fruit but froze when asked a question.

questions.text: What did the online tutor say about mistakes?
options: That they should be avoided at all costs
That they are how you learn
That they lose marks in a real exam
questions.explanation: The tutor kept saying that mistakes are how you learn.

questions.text: Why does Nam feel nervous about mistakes?
options: His friends all speak German much better
His teacher once laughed at him in front of others
At school a wrong answer meant a bad mark.
questions.explanation: At school wrong answers were punished with bad marks, so he still feels nervous.

evidence.quote: a wrong answer meant a bad mark

questions.text: Why does Sarah offer to send Nam the tutor's details?
options: She thinks a tutor will help him too.
She wants to sell him some lessons of her own
She is too busy to practise with him herself
questions.explanation: After hearing Nam's problem, she recommends her patient tutor.

questions.text: What does Professor Hill think about children learning two languages?
options: It is a bad idea until they have learnt to read
It rarely causes problems and can help them
It confuses them for ever, even as adults
questions.explanation: He says there is very little truth in the idea and children may even gain advantages.

evidence.quote: Very little, I'm happy to say.

questions.text: What does Professor Hill suggest about being fluent as an adult?
options: Confident communication is a realistic goal.
It is impossible unless you learn as a child
Sounding like a native speaker is quite easy
questions.explanation: Sounding like a native speaker is rare and unnecessary; confident communication is common.

questions.text: Why is translating every word not helpful?
options: It slows you down and words do not match exactly
It teaches grammar badly and confuses spelling
It is too easy and does not challenge the brain
questions.explanation: He says translation slows you down and one word can need several words in another language.

evidence.quote: Translating every word in your head slows you down

questions.text: Why does he suggest subtitles in the language you are studying?
options: So that you learn from what you read and hear
Because they are shorter and easier to follow
Because they are free on most streaming sites
questions.explanation: Reading only subtitles in your own language teaches little.

questions.text: What does Professor Hill say is the most useful habit?
options: One long session every Sunday afternoon
Memorising long vocabulary lists
Regular daily contact
questions.explanation: He says twenty minutes every day is worth more than a three-hour Sunday session.

evidence.quote: Twenty minutes every day is worth more than a three-hour session on Sunday

questions.text: What surprising thing does Mr Minh say at the start?
options: No course can teach a language on its own.
Students do not need to attend every lesson
The course is easier than it looks
questions.explanation: He says real learning happens in the students' own time.

evidence.quote: no course can teach you a language on its own

questions.text: Why does he suggest a fixed study time?
options: The school requires it.
It is cheaper.
It becomes automatic like a habit.
questions.explanation: Fixed time makes studying automatic, like brushing your teeth.

questions.text: Why does he mention the Thursday conversation club?
options: To collect the fees for the autumn course
To advertise a weekend trip with the teacher
To encourage students to speak from the start
questions.explanation: He recommends it because students should speak from the beginning.

questions.text: What is a plateau?
options: A kind of dictionary for advanced students
A type of exam given at the end of the course
A period when you feel you are not improving
questions.explanation: He explains it as days with no progress, often before a sudden jump forward.

questions.text: What will students do at the end of the talk?
options: Share their study plans in groups
Take a short test on today's lesson
Go to the conversation club together
questions.explanation: They fill in the sheet and share plans in groups of three.
